title: Which Multimedia Strategies Actually Improve Learning?
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick reviews a new meta-analysis pooling nearly three decades of Richard Mayer's multimedia learning research to ask which design strategies actually improve learning, and under what conditions. The overall effect is moderate (g=0.37), with the most reliable gains coming from stripping out seductive details, using the modality principle (spoken words plus visuals), personal/conversational language, and self-explanation prompts; plain text plus diagrams performs consistently well across factual, inferential, and transfer outcomes. By contrast, VR shows no significant overall advantage and animations, games, and simulations are inconsistent, helping more with inference and transfer than with simple fact recall. Hendrick explains these patterns through Mayer's three-process cognitive framework -- selection, organisation, and integration -- arguing that different multimedia principles support different cognitive processes, and that effects vary substantially by age, academic domain, and learning goal. He closes by situating the findings within a broader pattern of educational technology's benefits being oversold relative to careful, evidence-grounded implementation.
points: The meta-analysis's headline finding undercuts the tech-novelty narrative: plain text combined with diagrams is the most reliable multimedia approach across factual, inferential, and transfer outcomes, while VR shows no significant overall benefit.

Hendrick's three-process framework (select, organise, integrate) explains why different design principles work for different goals -- removing seductive details helps factual recall, structural scaffolds help inference, and self-explanation prompts help transfer.

Boundary conditions matter as much as the principles themselves: university and medical students benefited more than younger or graduate learners, and STEM/medical domains benefited more than liberal-arts subjects with less hierarchical knowledge structures.
Effect sizes have declined slightly over the publication period, which Hendrick reads as evidence that novelty-driven tech excitement fades while durable pedagogical principles do not.
quotes: If I was to sum up his work in one idea, it’s that clarity beats novelty, and that students learn by actually thinking hard about stuff, not merely being entertained.
Pooling Mayer’s studies from 1990–2022, the average impact is a respectable “medium” (g=0.37).

Text combined with diagrams emerged as the most reliable approach across all learning outcomes. This humble combination consistently produced meaningful learning gains whether students were trying to memorise facts, make inferences, or transfer knowledge to new situations.
Virtual reality, despite generating enormous excitement and investment, VR showed non-significant effects overall.
The decline in effect sizes over time is particularly sobering, suggesting that as multimedia becomes commonplace, its advantages may diminish.
For me, this research joins a growing body of evidence suggesting that educational technology's benefits have been oversold.
